prompt.context: Your client is a large global PE firm that has just acquired a trailer manufacturing company that manufactures open trailers. The PE firm owns another trailer manufacturing company that sells similar types of products. The deal has been approved so you don't need to worry about fit in portfolio, viability of the deal, etc. A good amount of cost synergies have already been identified (mostly procurement/purchasing savings) so we don't need to assess if there are any (this has already been done). The PE firm has engaged your team to help them think through what they should do now that they own both of these manufacturers and their respective brands.
prompt.question: What should the PE firm do now that it owns both trailer manufacturers and their respective brands?

clarifying_info.q: Who are the customers of these trailer manufacturers?
clarifying_info.a: Trailers are purchased by 3rd party dealers (similar to a car dealership). The dealers then sell the finished product to the end customer.

clarifying_info.q: How competitive is the open trailer market?
clarifying_info.a: The open trailer market is extremely fragmented. Both manufacturers combined own ~12% of the U.S. market and are considered two of the largest players. Most competitors are unsophisticated, usually 3-4 locations only. The market tracks the economy (commercial/industrial real estate) and has been growing at ~2% per year.

clarifying_info.q: How important is brand in this market?
clarifying_info.a: Brand is moderately important but quality of product is most important.

clarifying_info.q: Where does Trailer Co. A operate?
clarifying_info.a: Trailer Co. A operates exclusively in the Southwest of the United States.

clarifying_info.q: Where does Trailer Co. B operate?
clarifying_info.a: Trailer Co. B operates exclusively in the Northeast of the United States.

clarifying_info.q: How fast is Trailer Co. A growing?
clarifying_info.a: Trailer Co. A sales have been growing at a CAGR of ~15% versus market growth of ~2%.

clarifying_info.q: How fast is Trailer Co. B growing?
clarifying_info.a: Trailer Co. B sales have been growing at a CAGR of ~7% versus market growth of ~2%.

clarifying_info.q: What are the gross margins for each manufacturer?
clarifying_info.a: Trailer Co. A recently invested in a large CAPEX project to automate their assembly line and is extremely efficient at ~60% gross margin. Trailer Co. B still manufactures the majority of product by hand with relatively low automation, at ~40% gross margin.

clarifying_info.q: What is each company's dealer strategy?
clarifying_info.a: Trailer Co. A operates a large sales force to proactively acquire dealers ('land grab' strategy) with limited interaction once a dealer is added. Trailer Co. B is very opportunistic and passive in recruiting dealers, only targeting dealers with a defensible position and upside, and then provides extensive post-sale support (financing, marketing, inventory management) to help dealers reach their full potential.

clarifying_info.q: What type of product is an open trailer?
clarifying_info.a: An open trailer is essentially a flatbed trailer with wheels — sometimes with sides but the top is open. Materials are basic (wood, metal/steel, rubber). Not highly differentiable, though Trailer Co. B has nicer finishes (e.g., nicer tail lights).

exhibits.title: Competitive Landscape — Average Price per Trailer
exhibits.shows: A chart showing trailer manufacturers plotted by average price per unit (x-axis: increasing average price) with bar height indicating relative company revenue. Trailer Co. A and Trailer Co. B are highlighted alongside numerous regional competitors.

data.Regional Competitors (sample): prices ranging from $1.7K to $7.7K; heights indicate relative revenue

framework: Identify the binary decision: combine the two manufacturers vs. keep them separate
Understand the value chain: the real customers are the dealers, not end consumers — each manufacturer's strategy is defined by how it interacts with its dealer network
Characterize each manufacturer's current strategy: Trailer Co. A = high-volume 'land grab' transactional model; Trailer Co. B = selective 'cultivation' relationship model
Compare operational profiles: geography, growth rates, gross margins, product portfolio, price points, dealer network size/quality
Assess synergy potential without combination: procurement synergies already identified; evaluate additional levers (best-practice sharing, cross-sell)
Evaluate whether combining brands/operations creates net value or destroys it: geographic overlap, brand equity, channel conflict, strategic fit
Form a recommendation with clear justification and risks

questions.prompt: What are the two high-level options the PE firm faces, and what is your initial hypothesis?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates immediately frame the decision as binary: (1) merge/combine the two manufacturers or (2) keep them separate. A hypothesis should be stated early — e.g., 'My hypothesis is that the PE firm should keep the two manufacturers separate, because they serve different geographies and appear to have differentiated and working strategies. I want to test this by comparing their strategies, financials, and overlap.' Avoid meandering through generic frameworks before committing to a hypothesis.

questions.prompt: What is the total size of the U.S. open trailer market, given what you know about combined market share?
questions.guidance: Candidates should back into market size using the combined revenue of both manufacturers and the known market share. The PE firm's two companies together represent ~12% of the market. If revenues are provided (or derived from price x volume), total market = combined revenue / 0.12. This tests ability to back out implied figures from partial data.

math.setup: Combined revenue of Trailer Co. A + Trailer Co. B = ~12% of total U.S. open trailer market. Total market = (Co. A revenue + Co. B revenue) / 0.12
steps: Obtain or estimate each company's revenue from exhibit data (avg price x units) or from interviewer-provided figures
Sum revenues of Co. A and Co. B
Divide by 0.12 to get total market size
math.answer: Depends on revenue figures provided; if combined revenue is e.g. $X, then total market = $X / 0.12. Interviewers can tailor exact figures; the method is what matters.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit A, what observations can you make about the competitive positioning and pricing of Trailer Co. A and Trailer Co. B versus regional competitors?
questions.guidance: Trailer Co. A at $4.7K and Co. B at $5.9K are both in the mid-to-upper range of the price spectrum compared to regional competitors ($1.7K–$7.7K). Co. B's higher price point is consistent with its differentiated product (better finishes) and relationship-driven model. Most regional competitors are smaller (shorter bars) and lower-priced, reflecting their unsophisticated nature. The fragmented competitive landscape with many small, low-price players validates growth opportunity by taking share.

questions.prompt: How do the unit economics compare between Trailer Co. A and Trailer Co. B? Which manufacturer is more profitable per dealer?
questions.guidance: Candidates should use available data to compute or compare profit per dealer. Trailer Co. A has ~60% gross margin on a $4.7K average price = ~$2.8K gross profit per unit; Co. B has ~40% gross margin on a $5.9K average price = ~$2.4K gross profit per unit. However, Co. B's cultivation model is designed to produce higher revenue and profitability per dealer over time. Candidates should distinguish between per-unit margin and per-dealer profitability (dealer volume x margin per unit minus cost of support). The key insight is that Co. B's more expensive service model may produce superior per-dealer economics even at lower unit margins.

math.setup: Gross profit per unit = average price x gross margin %
steps: Co. A: $4.7K x 60% = $2.82K gross profit per trailer
Co. B: $5.9K x 40% = $2.36K gross profit per trailer
To compare per-dealer profitability, also consider number of units per dealer and cost of post-sale support for Co. B
math.answer: Co. A earns more gross profit per unit (~$2.82K vs ~$2.36K), but Co. B's higher-engagement model likely generates more revenue and profit per dealer over the dealer relationship lifetime.

brainstorming.prompt: If the PE firm decides to keep the two manufacturers separate but wants to share best practices, what specific practices could each company learn from the other?

categories.name: What Co. A can learn from Co. B
ideas: Dealer quality screening — selectively targeting dealers with defensible market positions rather than signing any dealer
Post-sale support playbook — offering financing, marketing, and inventory management support to improve dealer performance
Product differentiation — improving finishes and quality perception to support higher price points
Relationship management — deeper engagement to reduce dealer churn

categories.name: What Co. B can learn from Co. A
ideas: Scaling the dealer network — more proactive outreach to grow the dealer base faster
Operational automation — investing in manufacturing automation to improve gross margin from ~40% toward Co. A's ~60%
Sales force model — using a dedicated sales force to accelerate dealer acquisition
Volume-based efficiencies — leveraging greater scale in procurement and production

categories.name: Combined/shared initiatives
ideas: Procurement synergies on raw materials (wood, steel, rubber) — already identified
Cross-selling Co. B's additional product lines (consumer trailers, truck beds) through Co. A's larger dealer network
Shared management best practices and leadership development

recommendation: Keep the two manufacturers separate and operate them as distinct brands with their own strategies — do not merge.
Capture the already-identified procurement/purchasing cost synergies, which can be realized without combining the brands or manufacturing operations.

Implement a best-practice sharing program: Co. B's dealer cultivation playbook can improve Co. A's dealer quality over time; Co. A's automation and scaling model can inform Co. B's efficiency roadmap.
Optionally, explore cross-selling Co. B's differentiated product lines through Co. A's larger dealer network.
risks: Forgoing potential revenue synergies if the brands remain entirely siloed
Co. A's rapid dealer growth at low engagement may produce higher churn or lower dealer quality over time without adopting some of Co. B's cultivation practices
If the open trailer market consolidates, two separate smaller brands may be at a disadvantage versus a merged entity
Difficulty in sharing best practices without inadvertently blurring the distinct strategic identities of each brand
next_steps: Quantify procurement synergy capture timeline and track realization
Design a structured best-practice exchange program between the two management teams
Monitor dealer performance metrics for both networks to validate whether each strategy continues to outperform the market
Evaluate whether Co. B's product extensions (consumer trailers, truck beds) can be piloted through Co. A's Southwest dealer network
